743.title: When sakhis differ
743.hook: traditions sometimes tell the same story in different places; the lesson usually stays the same
743.howItsDone: Sikh teachers telling a sakhi may note that tellings differ, and the Guru Granth Sahib, not any janamsakhi, is treated as the Guru and final authority.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhumia's promises: three small vows that turned a robber around, because promises change us. Today, what to do when the tellings disagree.

At a family dinner, two cousins start telling the same story about their grandfather. One says it happened at the train station. The other says no, it was the market, and it was raining. They argue about the rain for five minutes. Then someone at the end of the table says: does it matter? He gave the man his coat either way. Everyone goes quiet, because that was the whole point of the story. The janamsakhis have dinners like that too.
screen: `THE STATION, OR THE MARKET?` → `HE GAVE THE COAT EITHER WAY.` → `THE JANAMSAKHIS HAVE DINNERS LIKE THAT.`

segments.voice: This block began with the janamsakhis and their families: the old Puratan telling, the Bala telling, Miharban's reflective one, the illustrated pages. They don't always agree. A sakhi set in one town in one collection may turn up somewhere else in another; a detail added in one is missing in the next. You've met it already: tellings place Mardana's death in different places, and differ on what the king did with Bhumia. How do you hold that? Go back to what a sakhi is: truth carried in the shape of a story. A news report lives or dies by where and when. A sakhi lives by what it teaches. So watch what stays put when the details move. Mardana refuses a tomb, wherever he dies. Bhumia's three promises hold, whatever the king decides. The differences have value, too. Historians compare tellings to learn which material looks older and how stories traveled; that work isn't an attack on the sakhis, it's a kind of care for them. And a teller who says, in some tellings it was here, in others there, is being honest. Sikh tradition gives its highest authority to the Guru Granth Sahib, not to any janamsakhi, so the stories can differ without the ground moving.

744.title: Painted sakhis
744.hook: sakhis became paintings, murals and later posters in Sikh homes
744.tomorrow: Telling a sakhi to a child
744.howItsDone: Sikh homes and gurdwaras may display paintings and prints of scenes from the Gurus' lives as reminders of the stories, while the bow in the gurdwara is made to the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sakhi: the details move between tellings, but the lesson stays. Today, the sakhis leave the page.

In a living room in Birmingham, or Fresno, or Ludhiana, there's a framed picture above the sofa. An old man with a white beard sits under a tree. On one side, a younger man holds a stringed instrument. On the other, a man waves a whisk over him. A child in that house has looked at it every day since before she could read. Ask her who they are, and she'll tell you. Nobody sat her down for a lesson. The wall did it.
screen: `A PICTURE ABOVE THE SOFA.` → `AN OLD MAN UNDER A TREE.` → `THE WALL TAUGHT HER.`

segments.voice: On day seven hundred twenty-six we met B40, a book with a painting beside each sakhi. A book sits on a shelf, and someone has to open it. Today the pictures leave the book. Sakhis went up on walls: murals painted inside gurdwaras and old houses, showing Nanak on the road, at the river, with the yogis on the mountain. Later came printed pictures, posters and calendars, cheap enough to hang in any home. That changes how a picture teaches. A page is seen when you sit down to read it. A wall is seen over and over without trying: on the way to breakfast, in the middle of an argument, on a sick day on the sofa. The girl in that living room never had a lesson. She had years of passing by. Look closer at her picture. The man with the whisk is Bhai Bala, the companion from the Bala tellings, the one historians still discuss. A print has no footnotes. It quietly carries one telling's choices into the house, and its faces are each artist's own imagining. So yesterday's habit works on walls too: ask what the picture knows, and which telling it comes from. Sikh teachers add a caution. A picture is a reminder of a story, not something to bow to. In the gurdwara, the bow goes to the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word. The picture points; it doesn't receive.

segments.voice: Look at a picture near you, a family photo, a print, a child's drawing on the fridge, or your phone's lock screen if the walls are bare. Ask what moment someone chose to keep, and what it teaches anyone who passes it every day. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath.

Your line: pictures teach. A wall can teach without a word. Day seven hundred forty-four.

745.title: Telling a sakhi to a child
745.hook: sakhis were first told aloud to children and sangats
745.howItsDone: Sikh families tell sakhis to children at home, and sakhis are told in gurdwaras in katha and in children's classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, painted sakhis: stories that moved from pages to walls, because pictures teach. Today, the oldest way a sakhi travels: out loud.

Again. Tell it again. Bedtime, the same story for the fourth night running, and a small voice under the blanket wants it once more. The child already knows how it ends. That isn't the point. The point is hearing it from you, in your voice, with the pause in the same place. Before sakhis were written in collections or painted on walls, they lived like that: spoken aloud, to children at home and to the sangat, the gathered community.
screen: `AGAIN. TELL IT AGAIN.` → `THE SAME PAUSE IN THE SAME PLACE.` → `SPOKEN BEFORE WRITTEN.`

segments.voice: Take a sakhi from the last few days and try it out loud. The two villages works well. Start with the road: Nanak and Mardana, dusty and hungry, walking into a village at dusk. Let the doors close. Let somebody laugh. Then the blessing: may you stay settled. Pause. Then the kind village, the bread for the road, and: may you scatter. Now the best part: let the child be Mardana. Wait. That's backward! Good tellers find the moment. A sakhi like this has a turn, where the surprise lives. Slow down there; rush the rest if you need to. They let the questions in. Mardana speaks up in these stories, and his objections can be the child's. When a child says that's not fair, the story is working. And they tell it true. Back on day seven hundred twenty, we said a story lives because someone tells it well and truly. With a child, that means saying tradition says when it's tradition, and it's fine to say, I don't know, some people tell it differently. Don't explain it to death. Say the lesson once, plainly, then stop. Unkindness stays where it is; goodness travels. Let the child carry the rest. That's how sakhis reached the sangat: not as a lecture, but as a voice in a room, and someone who'll ask for it again.

746.title: The sakhis close
746.hook: the travels, the tests, the laughter and the lessons
746.howItsDone: Sikhs return to the sakhis of Guru Nanak's life in katha, at gurpurab celebrations and at home, and families have favorites they tell again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangat, the gathered community where sakhis were told aloud, slow at the turn: pass it on. Today, we stop and look back down the road.

Boiling oil gone cool. A dead pipal tree turning green. Bitter soapnuts that tasted sweet. A pot cooking on an eclipse day while the crowd shouted. A boy watching kindling catch. A robber setting down treasure because he'd tasted salt. That's a lot of road for twenty-five days. This block opened the janamsakhis, the life-stories of Guru Nanak, and walked through them one sakhi at a time. Today we stop at the end of the road and look back.
screen: `OIL GONE COOL. SOAPNUTS MADE SWEET.` → `A ROBBER SETS DOWN THE TREASURE.` → `LOOKING BACK DOWN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Start with the books: the old Puratan telling, the Bala telling, Miharban's thoughtful one, the illustrated pages. We learned to read a sakhi not as a news report, but as truth in the shape of a story. Then the people around Nanak: Mata Sulakhni, who kept the home going; Sri Chand, who chose a different path; parents in Talwandi asking him to stay. Then the travels and the tests. Kauda and the oil. Mardana bewitched and sung free. Bitter fruit made sweet. The yogis' seat. Cooking at the eclipse. The learned man of Benares. Farid's verses kept at Pakpattan. The king of the island, waiting. Then endings and beginnings: Mardana's last song and the rabab handed on, a boy by the fire who became Baba Buddha, two villages, settle here, scatter there, and Bhumia's three promises. Last, how the sakhis live: differing in the details while the lesson stays, painted on walls, told aloud to children. Look across it all and a pattern shows. In these sakhis, the tests aren't won by force. The oil cools, the robber keeps his word, the pandit listens to a song. And there's laughter in it: a Guru blessing the rude village to stay home. Tomorrow the voices change. The Guru Granth Sahib holds the words of the Gurus and also of Bhagats, holy poets from different backgrounds. We met Kabir and Farid already. Next, the Bhagats in their own voices.

747.title: Fifteen voices
747.hook: Kabir, Farid, Namdev, Ravidas, Trilochan, Beni, Dhanna, Sain, Pipa, Sadhna, Ramanand, Parmanand, Surdas, Jaidev and Bhikhan
747.howItsDone: In gurdwaras the hymns of the bhagats are sung in kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib with the same honor as the Gurus' hymns, and the bhagat hymns carry their singers' names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the janamsakhis closed, and each of us kept a favorite sakhi. Today a new stretch of the road begins.

Kabir. Farid. Namdev. Ravidas. Trilochan. Beni. Dhanna. Sain. Pipa. Sadhna. Ramanand. Parmanand. Surdas. Jaidev. Bhikhan. Not one of those names belongs to a Sikh Guru. Some were Hindu devotees, some came from Muslim families, and by their own words several worked with their hands: a weaver, a man who carried dead cattle, a cloth printer. Yet their hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib, the book Sikhs bow to as their living Guru. For the next stretch, we meet these singers one by one. Today, all of them at once.
screen: `FIFTEEN NAMES, NO GURU AMONG THEM.` → `WEAVERS, PRINTERS, DEVOTEES.` → `INSIDE THE GURU'S OWN BOOK.`

segments.voice: Sikhs call them the bhagats, the devotees. Tradition says that when Guru Arjan gathered the hymns that became the Granth, he set the words of these saints beside the words of the Gurus. Where their hymns appear, they come at the end of a raag's section, after the Gurus' own: under the same musical headings, read in the same voice by the same granthi, bowed to the same way. In Raag Asa, at the start of Bhagat Dhanna's hymns, there's almost a roll call. Namdev, a calico printer worth half a copper coin, became worth a fortune. Kabir left his loom for love of the Lord's feet. Ravidas, who carried dead cattle, let go of the world's pull. Sain, the barber, became a devotee. And Dhanna, a farmer, hears all this and gets up to give his own life to devotion. That list doesn't open with a king or a priest. It opens with working people, named by their trades. The bhagat hymns sign themselves, too: near the end you'll hear Kahu Kabir, says Kabir, or Kahi Ravidas, says Ravidas. The voices stay distinct. Their accents and languages differ; some lines sound like a village and some like a court. Yet in the Sikh telling there isn't a front section for the Gurus and a back shelf for guests. The whole book together is the Guru.

748.title: The weaver of Benares
748.hook: Kabir, a weaver of Kashi, sang the Lord's name in the plain speech of the street
748.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Kabir's hymns in kirtan alongside the Gurus' hymns, and his signature 'says Kabir' is heard in gurdwaras in raag after raag.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fifteen voices: saints of many backgrounds, side by side with the Gurus in one book. Today we sit down beside the first of them, at his loom.

Clack. Shuttle across. Clack. Beater down. Clack. In the old city of Kashi, also called Benares or Varanasi, a man sits at a loom set into the floor, feet on the pedals, hands throwing the shuttle back and forth, all day. Thread in, cloth out. Somewhere in that rhythm, he starts to sing. And the songs he made at work, or so tradition tells it, travel further than any cloth he ever sold. Some of them end up inside the Guru Granth Sahib. His name is Kabir, and today's word is what he did for a living.
screen: `CLACK. SHUTTLE ACROSS.` → `A LOOM IN KASHI.` → `A MAN SINGS AT WORK.`

segments.voice: Julaha. A weaver. It's not a title somebody gave Kabir later; he uses it about himself. In a hymn in Raag Asa, Kabir speaks to a Brahmin and says, in plain words: you are a Brahmin, and I am a weaver of Kashi. Then he asks the man to grasp what he's saying. He doesn't hide the trade. A weaver in that world was a working man, and some looked down on the work. Kabir sets it right there in the hymn, next to his name, like a signature. Tradition says he grew up in a Muslim family of weavers, and the hymns sing of Ram and Hari, of Allah and the One beyond every name. Sikhs honor him as a bhagat, a devotee of the One. Then there's his language. Kabir's hymns in the Granth often sound less like a temple or a court than like a lane in a market: pots, threads, cows, a dog, a mother, a loom. He took the things in front of him and made them carry God. And here's the turn. Yesterday's roll call in Raag Asa said Kabir left his loom for love of the Lord's feet. Yet the loom never leaves his songs. The work becomes the picture. Whatever he sings about the Lord, he often sings it with a weaver's hands: devotion at the level of the shuttle and the thread.

749.title: Warp and weft
749.hook: Kabir pictures the world as cloth on the Lord's loom, and the body as the place the weaver comes home
749.howItsDone: Sikhs sing and reflect on Kabir's loom hymns in kirtan and katha, reading the weaver and the cloth as pictures of the Creator, the world and the soul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, julaha: Kabir called himself a weaver, and sang his devotion at the level of the thread, a weaver's song. Today the whole universe goes on his loom.

Pull a thread from the hem of your sleeve and you'll find it isn't alone. Every piece of cloth is two sets of thread. One is stretched long and tight on the loom before anything begins: that's the warp. The other runs across it, over and under, carried by the shuttle: that's the weft. Neither one is cloth by itself. Only crossed do they hold. Kabir knew this the way a cook knows salt. And in one hymn he takes the whole loom, frame and thread and shuttle, and hangs the universe on it.
screen: `TWO SETS OF THREAD.` → `THE WARP, STRETCHED LONG.` → `THE WEFT, CARRIED ACROSS.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Asa, and it begins with a riddle. Nobody, Kabir says, knows the secret of the Weaver, who has stretched out the whole world as his warp. God here is not a king on a throne. God is a weaver, and the world is the long thread on the frame. Then it widens. The earth and the sky are made into the loom. The sun and the moon move across together, like the shuttles going back and forth. You can almost hear it: day, night, day, night, the weft running across the warp. There's even a little jab in it. While you sat listening to the Vedas and the Puranas, he says, I stretched out this much of my warp. I was working, and the work was teaching me. Then the hymn turns inward. The weaver, Kabir sings, came to know his own home, and recognized the Lord right inside the body. The loom outside became the loom within. And it ends at the end of a life. When the loom is broken, he says, the weaver merges thread into thread. The cloth comes off the frame, and the thread goes back to the thread it came from. Some readers hear in this the soul returning to the One it was always part of. Nothing in the picture is wasted, and nothing is separate: crossed, over and under, until it holds.

segments.voice: Bring a piece of cloth close to your eyes, a sleeve, a towel, the knee of your jeans, and find the threads running one way, then the threads crossing them. Follow one thread as far as you can before it slips under another, and notice that it never stops being itself, and never stops holding the others. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly as you trace it.
